lines.text: 1. Securing Layer 2 Technologies
lines.spoken: 1. Securing Layer 2 Technologies.

lines.text: Why Review Layer 2
lines.spoken: Why Review Layer 2.

lines.text: Layer 2 is often taken for granted because ARP and Ethernet forwarding just work.
lines.spoken: Layer 2 is often taken for granted because arp and Ethernet forwarding just work.

lines.text: The CCNP and CCIE Security exams assume you know VLANs, trunking, and inter-VLAN routing. The chapter reviews them so the later mitigation section makes sense.
lines.spoken: The C.C.N.P. and CCIE Security exams assume you know V-lans, trunking, and inter-V-lan routing. The chapter reviews them so the later mitigation section makes sense.

lines.text: Figure 6-1 topology: router R1 connects to SW1 on Gi0/1. SW1 links to SW2 (SW1 Gi0/3 to SW2 Gi0/1). Host A (VLAN 10) is on SW1 Gi0/2. Host B (VLAN 20) is on SW2 Gi0/2. The STP examples instead show the switches linked on ports 23 and 24.

lines.text: VLANs
lines.spoken: V-lans.

lines.text: A LAN is all devices sharing one Layer 3 network address and one Layer 2 broadcast domain.
lines.spoken: A lan is all devices sharing one Layer 3 network address and one Layer 2 broadcast domain.

lines.text: In the default configuration every port is in VLAN 1, so both users and the router share one broadcast domain.
lines.spoken: In the default configuration every port is in V-lan 1, so both users and the router share one broadcast domain.

lines.text: With hundreds of users, separate groups into individual subnets, each with its own VLAN.
lines.spoken: With hundreds of users, separate groups into individual subnets, each with its own V-lan.

lines.text: Devices in a VLAN should share an IP subnet. DHCP often assigns addresses from it.
lines.spoken: Devices in a V-lan should share an IP subnet. DHCP often assigns addresses from it.

lines.text: VLANs can also be assigned to wireless clients to enforce policy (from Chapter 5).
lines.spoken: V-lans can also be assigned to wireless clients to enforce policy (from Chapter 5).

lines.text: Trunking
lines.spoken: Trunking.

lines.text: Two users in the same VLAN on different switches can't talk until the inter-switch links are trunks.
lines.spoken: Two users in the same V-lan on different switches can't talk until the inter-switch links are trunks.

lines.text: Following the frame: a broadcast from Host A enters SW1 in VLAN 10, crosses the trunk tagged VLAN 10, and SW2 removes the tag and floods it to its VLAN 10 ports. The book says SW2 sees "a broadcast associated with VLAN 20" and forwards it to Host B, which contradicts the VLAN 10 tag in the same sentence.
lines.spoken: Following the frame: a broadcast from Host A enters S.W. 1 in V-lan 10, crosses the trunk tagged V-lan 10, and S.W. 2 removes the tag and floods it to its V-lan 10 ports. The book says S.W. 2 sees "a broadcast associated with V-lan 20" and forwards it to Host B, which contradicts the V-lan 10 tag in the same sentence.

lines.text: Access ports in one VLAN, plus trunks that tag frames, are the core building blocks that let a VLAN extend beyond one switch.
lines.spoken: Access ports in one V-lan, plus trunks that tag frames, are the core building blocks that let a V-lan extend beyond one switch.

lines.text: Native VLAN frames are sent untagged when both switches agree on the same native VLAN. Attackers can abuse this, so use a dedicated native VLAN other than VLAN 1 and never use it for user traffic.
lines.spoken: Native V-lan frames are sent untagged when both switches agree on the same native V-lan. Attackers can abuse this, so use a dedicated native V-lan other than V-lan 1 and never use it for user traffic.

lines.text: Automatic trunk negotiation is risky because an attacker's PC could negotiate a trunk and tag its way into any VLAN.
lines.spoken: Automatic trunk negotiation is risky because an attacker's P.C. could negotiate a trunk and tag its way into any V-lan.

lines.text: Inter-VLAN Routing
lines.spoken: Inter-V-lan Routing.

lines.text: Hosts need a default gateway to leave their VLAN.
lines.spoken: Hosts need a default gateway to leave their V-lan.

lines.text: A router with one physical interface per VLAN works but doesn't scale: 50 VLANs would need 50 router interfaces and 50 switch ports.
lines.spoken: A router with one physical interface per V-lan works but doesn't scale: 50 V-lans would need 50 router interfaces and 50 switch ports.

lines.text: Router-on-a-stick solves this. The switch trunks to the router exactly as it would to another switch, and the router maps each VLAN tag to a sub-interface.
lines.spoken: Router-on-a-stick solves this. The switch trunks to the router exactly as it would to another switch, and the router maps each V-lan tag to a sub-interface.

lines.text: Repeat sub-interfaces until the router has one in every VLAN you want.
lines.spoken: Repeat sub-interfaces until the router has one in every V-lan you want.

lines.text: Spanning Tree Operation
lines.spoken: Spanning Tree Operation.

lines.text: STP is on by default on most Cisco switches.
lines.spoken: STP is on by default on most Cisco switches.

lines.text: Life of a loop without STP: Host A's ARP broadcast leaves SW1 on port 23, SW2 floods it out port 24 back to SW1, and SW1 sends it out port 23 again. The same happens in the other direction.
lines.spoken: Life of a loop without STP: Host A's arp broadcast leaves S.W. 1 on port 23, S.W. 2 floods it out port 24 back to S.W. 1, and S.W. 1 sends it out port 23 again. The same happens in the other direction.

lines.text: Trunk ports allow all VLANs by default, so the broadcast is tagged and carried on every trunk.
lines.spoken: Trunk ports allow all V-lans by default, so the broadcast is tagged and carried on every trunk.

lines.text: Non-root switches block all but one of their parallel paths to the root.
lines.spoken: Non-root switches block all but one of their parallel paths to the root.

lines.text: If every switch uses the default priority, the lowest MAC address becomes root.
lines.spoken: If every switch uses the default priority, the lowest mac address becomes root.

lines.text: In Example 6-12, SW1 (MAC 0019.060c.9080) beats SW2 (0019.0617.6600) because .060c is lower than .0617.
lines.spoken: In Example 6-12, S.W. 1 (mac 0019.060c.9080) beats S.W. 2 (0019.0617.6600) because .060c is lower than .0617.

lines.text: SW2 adds its local interface cost of 19 to the advertised cost of 0, so its cost to root is 19.
lines.spoken: S.W. 2 adds its local interface cost of 19 to the advertised cost of 0, so its cost to root is 19.

lines.text: SW2 hears BPDUs on both 23 and 24 at equal cost, so it uses the sender's port priority and picks the lower value. It blocks port 24. In STP, lower is always preferred, and lower-numbered ports have lower port priorities by default.
lines.spoken: S.W. 2 hears B.P.D.U.s on both 23 and 24 at equal cost, so it uses the sender's port priority and picks the lower value. It blocks port 24. In STP, lower is always preferred, and lower-numbered ports have lower port priorities by default.

lines.text: The blocking shows in show interfaces trunk: port 24 forwards for no VLANs, while port 23 forwards VLANs 1 and 10.
lines.spoken: The blocking shows in show interfaces trunk: port 24 forwards for no V-lans, while port 23 forwards V-lans 1 and 10.

lines.text: The book calls root, designated, and nondesignated "port states". They are really port roles. The actual 802.1D states (blocking, listening, learning, forwarding, disabled) are not listed together in the book, though it describes listening, learning, forwarding, and blocking.
lines.spoken: The book calls root, designated, and nondesignated "port states". They are really port roles. The actual 802.1D states (blocking, listening, learning, forwarding, disabled) are not listed together in the book, though it describes listening, learning, forwarding, and blocking.

lines.text: Time Until Forwarding
lines.spoken: Time Until Forwarding.

lines.text: A new port waits 30 seconds before forwarding, in case another switch is attached and creates a loop.
lines.spoken: A new port waits 30 seconds before forwarding, in case another switch is attached and creates a loop.

lines.text: PortFast skips the wait but leaves a small window for a loop if someone adds a parallel path.
lines.spoken: PortFast skips the wait but leaves a small window for a loop if someone adds a parallel path.

lines.text: 2. Common Layer 2 Threats and How to Mitigate Them
lines.spoken: 2. Common Layer 2 Threats and How to Mitigate Them.

lines.text: Disrupt the Bottom of the Wall
lines.spoken: Disrupt the Bottom of the Wall.

lines.text: Everything at Layer 3 and above is carried in a Layer 2 frame.
lines.spoken: Everything at Layer 3 and above is carried in a Layer 2 frame.

lines.text: An attacker who can interrupt, copy, redirect, or confuse Layer 2 forwarding disrupts every upper-layer protocol too.
lines.spoken: An attacker who can interrupt, copy, redirect, or confuse Layer 2 forwarding disrupts every upper-layer protocol too.

lines.text: Layer 2 Best Practices
lines.spoken: Layer 2 Best Practices.

lines.text: Use an unused VLAN other than VLAN 1 as the native VLAN on all trunks, and never on enabled access ports.
lines.spoken: Use an unused V-lan other than V-lan 1 as the native V-lan on all trunks, and never on enabled access ports.

lines.text: Avoid VLAN 1 anywhere, because it is a default.
lines.spoken: Avoid V-lan 1 anywhere, because it is a default.

lines.text: Hard-code access ports as access ports and disable trunk negotiation (no DTP).
lines.spoken: Hard-code access ports as access ports and disable trunk negotiation (no DTP).

lines.text: Limit MAC addresses per port with port security.
lines.spoken: Limit mac addresses per port with port security.

lines.text: Control spanning tree with BPDU Guard and Root Guard so users and unknown devices can't manipulate it.
lines.spoken: Control spanning tree with BPDU Guard and Root Guard so users and unknown devices can't manipulate it.

lines.text: Turn off CDP on ports facing untrusted or unknown networks that don't need it.
lines.spoken: Turn off CDP on ports facing untrusted or unknown networks that don't need it.

lines.text: On a new switch, shut down all ports and put them in a parking-lot VLAN. Bring them up and assign the right VLAN only as they are needed.
lines.spoken: On a new switch, shut down all ports and put them in a parking-lot V-lan. Bring them up and assign the right V-lan only as they are needed.

lines.text: Do Not Allow Negotiations
lines.spoken: Do Not Allow Negotiations.

lines.text: Forcing access mode with no negotiation stops a user from maliciously negotiating a trunk with custom dot1q software and VLAN hopping.
lines.spoken: Forcing access mode with no negotiation stops a user from maliciously negotiating a trunk with custom dot1q software and V-lan hopping.

lines.text: Trunks are also hard-coded and set to nonegotiate.
lines.spoken: Trunks are also hard-coded and set to nonegotiate.

lines.text: Layer 2 Security Toolkit
lines.spoken: Layer 2 Security Toolkit.

lines.text: BPDU Guard, Root Guard, port security, DHCP snooping, Dynamic ARP Inspection, IP Source Guard, 802.1X, Storm Control, and access control lists (for traffic control and policy).
lines.spoken: BPDU Guard, Root Guard, port security, DHCP snooping, Dynamic arp Inspection, IP Source Guard, 802 dot 1 X, Storm Control, and access control lists (for traffic control and policy).

lines.text: The chapter's focus: BPDU Guard, Root Guard, port security, CDP and LLDP, and DHCP snooping.
lines.spoken: The chapter's focus: BPDU Guard, Root Guard, port security, CDP and LLDP, and DHCP snooping.

lines.text: BPDU Guard
lines.spoken: BPDU Guard.

lines.text: Apply it only to ports that should connect to end stations.
lines.spoken: Apply it only to ports that should connect to end stations.

lines.text: Stops someone attaching another switch that sends BPDUs and changes the STP topology.
lines.spoken: Stops someone attaching another switch that sends B.P.D.U.s and changes the STP topology.

lines.text: Root Guard
lines.spoken: Root Guard.

lines.text: Use it on ports to switches you don't manage.
lines.spoken: Use it on ports to switches you don't manage.

lines.text: Prevents tampering with the existing STP topology.
lines.spoken: Prevents tampering with the existing STP topology.

lines.text: Port Security
lines.spoken: Port Security.

lines.text: A typical user has one MAC. Legitimate extras: a virtual machine or two, or an IP phone with a built-in switch.
lines.spoken: A typical user has one mac. Legitimate extras: a virtual machine or two, or an IP phone with a built-in switch.

lines.text: Stops a user from connecting dozens of devices through a rogue switch.
lines.spoken: Stops a user from connecting dozens of devices through a rogue switch.

lines.text: Stops CAM table overflow attacks.
lines.spoken: Stops cam table overflow attacks.

lines.text: Stops DHCP pool exhaustion through thousands of requests with different source MACs.
lines.spoken: Stops DHCP pool exhaustion through thousands of requests with different source macs.

lines.text: Violation actions:
lines.spoken: Violation actions:

lines.text: Shutdown: the default. Err-disables the port.
lines.spoken: Shutdown: the default. Err-disables the port.

lines.text: Protect: keeps the port up but drops frames from new MACs over the limit.
lines.spoken: Protect: keeps the port up but drops frames from new macs over the limit.

lines.text: Restrict: same as protect, plus a syslog message.
lines.spoken: Restrict: same as protect, plus a syslog message.

lines.text: CDP and LLDP
lines.spoken: CDP and LLDP.

lines.text: CDP runs on Cisco routers, switches, and phones and is licensed to some other vendors.
lines.spoken: CDP runs on Cisco routers, switches, and phones and is licensed to some other vendors.

lines.text: Applications such as voice came to depend on discovery protocols, which caused interoperability problems between vendors. That led to the standard, LLDP.
lines.spoken: Applications such as voice came to depend on discovery protocols, which caused interoperability problems between vendors. That led to the standard, LLDP.

lines.text: Disable CDP where it isn't needed, and likewise disable LLDP where it isn't needed.
lines.spoken: Disable CDP where it isn't needed, and likewise disable LLDP where it isn't needed.

lines.text: The book says Example 6-18 shows disabling CDP. It is actually Example 6-19; 6-18 is port security.
lines.spoken: The book says Example 6-18 shows disabling CDP. It is actually Example 6-19; 6-18 is port security.

lines.text: DHCP Snooping
lines.spoken: DHCP Snooping.

lines.text: What it does:
lines.spoken: What it does:

lines.text: Validates DHCP messages from untrusted sources and filters out invalid ones.
lines.spoken: Validates DHCP messages from untrusted sources and filters out invalid ones.

lines.text: Rate-limits DHCP traffic from trusted and untrusted sources.
lines.spoken: Rate-limits DHCP traffic from trusted and untrusted sources.

lines.text: Builds and maintains the binding database.
lines.spoken: Builds and maintains the binding database.

lines.text: Uses the database to validate later requests from untrusted hosts.
lines.spoken: Uses the database to validate later requests from untrusted hosts.

lines.text: Enabled per VLAN, and inactive on all VLANs by default. One VLAN or a range.
lines.spoken: Enabled per V-lan, and inactive on all V-lans by default. One V-lan or a range.

lines.text: Implementation steps:
lines.spoken: Implementation steps:

lines.text: 1. Define and configure the DHCP server. Not done on the switch and beyond the book's scope.
lines.spoken: 1. Define and configure the DHCP server. Not done on the switch and beyond the book's scope.

lines.text: 2. Enable DHCP snooping globally.
lines.spoken: 2. Enable DHCP snooping globally.

lines.text: 3. Enable it on at least one VLAN.
lines.spoken: 3. Enable it on at least one V-lan.

lines.text: 4. Make sure the DHCP server connects through a trusted interface.
lines.spoken: 4. Make sure the DHCP server connects through a trusted interface.

lines.text: 5. Configure the snooping database agent so entries are restored after a restart or switchover.
lines.spoken: 5. Configure the snooping database agent so entries are restored after a restart or switchover.

lines.text: The book says the feature is not active until step 5 is done. Its verification output shows VLAN 10 configured but "operational on following VLANs: none".
lines.spoken: The book says the feature is not active until step 5 is done. Its verification output shows V-lan 10 configured but "operational on following V-lans: none".

lines.text: Also stops a rogue DHCP server from handing out a false default gateway.
lines.spoken: Also stops a rogue DHCP server from handing out a false default gateway.

lines.text: Dynamic ARP Inspection
lines.spoken: Dynamic arp Inspection.

lines.text: Normal ARP: Host B broadcasts a request for Host A's MAC, every host receives it, and Host A answers.
lines.spoken: Normal arp: Host B broadcasts a request for Host A's mac, every host receives it, and Host A answers.

lines.text: Figure 6-2 attack: Hosts A (IA, MA), B (IB, MB), and C (IC, MC) share one subnet. When A and B exchange ARP, the switch and hosts cache IA to MA and IB to MB.
lines.spoken: Figure 6-2 attack: Hosts A (IA, MA), B (IB, MB), and C (IC, MC) share one subnet. When A and B exchange arp, the switch and hosts cache IA to MA and IB to MB.

lines.text: Host C broadcasts forged replies binding IA and IB to MC. Traffic for A and B goes to C, which forwards it with the true MACs. Host C is now a classic man-in-the-middle.
lines.spoken: Host C broadcasts forged replies binding IA and IB to MC. Traffic for A and B goes to C, which forwards it with the true macs. Host C is now a classic man-in-the-middle.

lines.text: After the attack, all traffic from the victim flows through the attacker to the router, switch, or host.
lines.spoken: After the attack, all traffic from the victim flows through the attacker to the router, switch, or host.

lines.text: DAI validates ARP against the DHCP snooping binding database, which exists only if DHCP snooping is enabled on the switch and VLANs.
lines.spoken: DAI validates arp against the DHCP snooping binding database, which exists only if DHCP snooping is enabled on the switch and V-lans.

lines.text: Trusted interfaces forward ARP without checks. Untrusted interfaces forward only valid packets.
lines.spoken: Trusted interfaces forward arp without checks. Untrusted interfaces forward only valid packets.

lines.text: DAI can also drop ARP with invalid IP addresses, or where the MACs in the ARP body don't match the Ethernet header.
lines.spoken: DAI can also drop arp with invalid IP addresses, or where the macs in the arp body don't match the Ethernet header.

lines.text: Protects against some man-in-the-middle attacks.
lines.spoken: Protects against some man-in-the-middle attacks.

lines.text: 3. Network Foundation Protection
lines.spoken: 3. Network Foundation Protection.

lines.text: Why the Infrastructure Matters
lines.spoken: Why the Infrastructure Matters.

lines.text: The infrastructure is mainly routers, switches, and cables. One broken component can fail the network, hurting revenue, productivity, other systems, and customers.
lines.spoken: The infrastructure is mainly routers, switches, and cables. One broken component can fail the network, hurting revenue, productivity, other systems, and customers.

lines.text: Weak or missing passwords, software vulnerabilities, and misconfigured devices leave the door open to attackers.
lines.spoken: Weak or missing passwords, software vulnerabilities, and misconfigured devices leave the door open to attackers.

lines.text: NFP breaks a big problem into smaller components and secures each systematically.
lines.spoken: NFP breaks a big problem into smaller components and secures each systematically.

lines.text: The Three Planes
lines.spoken: The Three Planes.

lines.text: The management plane is listed first because a device isn't very functional until it is configured.
lines.spoken: The management plane is listed first because a device isn't very functional until it is configured.

lines.text: If the data plane fails, customer traffic can't be forwarded. Policy may also deny some traffic in the data plane.
lines.spoken: If the data plane fails, customer traffic can't be forwarded. Policy may also deny some traffic in the data plane.

lines.text: Interdependence
lines.spoken: Interdependence.

lines.text: A control plane failure stops data plane forwarding because the router doesn't know where to send traffic.
lines.spoken: A control plane failure stops data plane forwarding because the router doesn't know where to send traffic.

lines.text: A management plane failure can let an attacker reconfigure devices and break both the control and data planes.
lines.spoken: A management plane failure can let an attacker reconfigure devices and break both the control and data planes.

lines.text: Security Measures per Plane (Table 6-2)
lines.spoken: Security Measures per Plane (Table 6-2).

lines.text: Management plane: AAA, authenticated NTP, SSH, TLS, protected syslog, SNMPv3, and NETCONF/RESTCONF.
lines.spoken: Management plane: triple A, authenticated N.T.P., SSH, TLS, protected syslog, SNMPv3, and net-conf or rest-conf.

lines.text: Control plane: CoPP, CPPr, and authenticated routing protocol updates.
lines.spoken: Control plane: cop, C.P.P.R., and authenticated routing protocol updates.

lines.text: Data plane: ACLs, Layer 2 controls (private VLANs and STP guards), Cisco IOS and IOS-XE Zone-Based Firewall, and SD-WAN security.
lines.spoken: Data plane: A.C.L.s, Layer 2 controls (private V-lans and STP guards), Cisco I.O.S. and I.O.S. X.E. Zone-Based Firewall, and S.D. wan security.

lines.text: Limits of NFP
lines.spoken: Limits of NFP.

lines.text: NFP won't keep the network up forever. Poor design with no fault tolerance still fails when a device, cable, or software breaks.
lines.spoken: NFP won't keep the network up forever. Poor design with no fault tolerance still fails when a device, cable, or software breaks.

lines.text: Lack of change control and accidental misconfiguration remain ongoing risks.
lines.spoken: Lack of change control and accidental misconfiguration remain ongoing risks.

lines.text: 4. Understanding and Securing the Management Plane
lines.spoken: 4. Understanding and Securing the Management Plane.

lines.text: Configuration Comes First
lines.spoken: Configuration Comes First.

lines.text: A device needs a working configuration from an administrator (console or SSH) or a management system such as Cisco DNA Center.
lines.spoken: A device needs a working configuration from an administrator (console or SSH) or a management system such as Cisco DNA Center.

lines.text: A basic Layer 2 switch with all ports in one VLAN would work but is unlikely to be the desired configuration.
lines.spoken: A basic Layer 2 switch with all ports in one V-lan would work but is unlikely to be the desired configuration.

lines.text: Best Practices
lines.spoken: Best Practices.

lines.text: Enforce a password policy, such as maximum login attempts and minimum password length.
lines.spoken: Enforce a password policy, such as maximum login attempts and minimum password length.

lines.text: Implement RBAC. A role is like a group: it carries permissions, and users assigned to it inherit them. Implement with ACS, CLI parser views, or custom privilege levels.
lines.spoken: Implement R-back. A role is like a group: it carries permissions, and users assigned to it inherit them. Implement with ACS, CLI parser views, or custom privilege levels.

lines.text: Use AAA, centrally managed on a server such as Cisco ISE. The device asks the server before any login or command, and the server keeps an audit trail of who logged in and what they ran.
lines.spoken: Use triple A, centrally managed on a server such as Cisco ice. The device asks the server before any login or command, and the server keeps an audit trail of who logged in and what they ran.

lines.text: Keep accurate time on all devices with secure NTP.
lines.spoken: Keep accurate time on all devices with secure N.T.P.

lines.text: Use encrypted and authenticated SNMP: Version 3, and some features from Version 2.
lines.spoken: Use encrypted and authenticated SNMP: Version 3, and some features from Version 2.

lines.text: Control which IP addresses may start management sessions.
lines.spoken: Control which IP addresses may start management sessions.

lines.text: Lock down syslog:
lines.spoken: Lock down syslog:

lines.text: Syslog is plain text. Permit it only between the device and its configured syslog destinations.
lines.spoken: Syslog is plain text. Permit it only between the device and its configured syslog destinations.

lines.text: Encryption is better, but few people do it.
lines.spoken: Encryption is better, but few people do it.

lines.text: Short of encryption, use out-of-band management, such as a separate management VLAN that user traffic never touches.
lines.spoken: Short of encryption, use out-of-band management, such as a separate management V-lan that user traffic never touches.

lines.text: In-band management traffic must be encrypted, natively or with IPsec.
lines.spoken: In-band management traffic must be encrypted, natively or with I.P. sec.

lines.text: Disable unneeded services, especially UDP ones, which are rarely legitimate and can be used for DoS:
lines.spoken: Disable unneeded services, especially UDP ones, which are rarely legitimate and can be used for D.O.S.:

lines.text: TCP and UDP small services, Finger, BOOTP, DHCP, MOP (Maintenance Operation Protocol), DNS, PAD (packet assembler/disassembler), HTTP and HTTPS servers, CDP, and LLDP.
lines.spoken: TCP and UDP small services, Finger, boot P, DHCP, mop (Maintenance Operation Protocol), DNS, pad (packet assembler or disassembler), HTTP and HTTPS servers, CDP, and LLDP.

lines.text: 5. Understanding the Control Plane
lines.spoken: 5. Understanding the Control Plane.

lines.text: Why the CPU Needs Protection
lines.spoken: Why the CPU Needs Protection.

lines.text: The router caches forwarding information so transit packets cost the CPU little. This mostly benefits the data plane.
lines.spoken: The router caches forwarding information so transit packets cost the CPU little. This mostly benefits the data plane.

lines.text: A packet addressed to the router itself, such as an OSPF or EIGRP advertisement, can't be forwarded from cache. The CPU must interpret it, read application data, and maybe respond.
lines.spoken: A packet addressed to the router itself, such as an OSPF or EIGRP advertisement, can't be forwarded from cache. The CPU must interpret it, read application data, and maybe respond.

lines.text: Thousands of such packets, or a botnet of hundreds of thousands of devices, can exhaust the router.
lines.spoken: Thousands of such packets, or a botnet of hundreds of thousands of devices, can exhaust the router.

lines.text: Control plane security mainly guards against attacks that hurt the CPU, including routing updates.
lines.spoken: Control plane security mainly guards against attacks that hurt the CPU, including routing updates.

lines.text: CoPP and CPPr Basics
lines.spoken: cop and C.P.P.R. Basics.

lines.text: CoPP can police management traffic such as SSH, HTTPS, and SSL to a set level or drop it. Excess traffic over the threshold is ignored, not processed by the CPU.
lines.spoken: cop can police management traffic such as SSH, HTTPS, and SSL to a set level or drop it. Excess traffic over the threshold is ignored, not processed by the CPU.

lines.text: Think of it as QoS for valid management traffic and policing for bogus management traffic.
lines.spoken: Think of it as QoS for valid management traffic and policing for bogus management traffic.

lines.text: Because CoPP and CPPr sit on the logical control plane interface, they protect the processor no matter which physical or logical interface a packet arrives on.
lines.spoken: Because cop and C.P.P.R. sit on the logical control plane interface, they protect the processor no matter which physical or logical interface a packet arrives on.

lines.text: CPPr sub-interfaces:
lines.spoken: C.P.P.R. sub-interfaces:

lines.text: Host sub-interface: traffic to one of the router's physical or logical interfaces.
lines.spoken: Host sub-interface: traffic to one of the router's physical or logical interfaces.

lines.text: Transit sub-interface: data plane traffic needing CPU help before forwarding, such as IP options.
lines.spoken: Transit sub-interface: data plane traffic needing CPU help before forwarding, such as IP options.

lines.text: CEF exception sub-interface: network operations traffic, such as keepalives or packets with expiring TTL.
lines.spoken: CEF exception sub-interface: network operations traffic, such as keepalives or packets with expiring TTL.

lines.text: Policy example: allow SSH at 100 packets per second and syslog at 200 packets per second. Drop traffic over the thresholds unless it comes from your management stations.
lines.spoken: Policy example: allow SSH at 100 packets per second and syslog at 200 packets per second. Drop traffic over the thresholds unless it comes from your management stations.

lines.text: Other Control Plane Practices
lines.spoken: Other Control Plane Practices.

lines.text: Routing protocol authentication: authorized routers won't believe a rogue router that tries to pull traffic through itself or learn the routing tables.
lines.spoken: Routing protocol authentication: authorized routers won't believe a rogue router that tries to pull traffic through itself or learn the routing tables.

lines.text: SPD protects the route processor from traffic sent to starve it.
lines.spoken: SPD protects the route processor from traffic sent to starve it.

lines.text: 6. Understanding and Securing the Data Plane
lines.spoken: 6. Understanding and Securing the Data Plane.

lines.text: Best Practices
lines.spoken: Best Practices.
